title: Transaction Isolation Levels
tagline: Dirty reads, phantom rows, and the spectrum of isolation that keeps concurrent transactions from stepping on each other.

sections.content:
Imagine two bank tellers working at adjacent windows, both accessing the same account at the same moment. One is reading the balance while the other is updating it. If they both proceed without any coordination, the bank can end up in an inconsistent state — a customer's balance might be double-credited, never decremented, or read mid-update as some nonsensical intermediate value. This is not a hypothetical: it is precisely what happens when a database handles hundreds or thousands of concurrent transactions without careful isolation rules.

A **transaction** is a unit of work that obeys the **ACID** properties: Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (valid state in and out), Isolation (concurrent transactions appear sequential), and Durability (committed data survives crashes). The isolation property is the most nuanced — and the most expensive to enforce fully. Rather than provide a single "isolated" mode, SQL defines a **spectrum of four isolation levels**, each making different trade-offs between correctness and concurrency.

The four levels — **Read Uncommitted**, **Read Committed**, **Repeatable Read**, and **Serializable** — are defined by the SQL standard in terms of three classic anomalies: **dirty reads**, **non-repeatable reads**, and **phantom reads**. Real systems also have to deal with anomalies the standard never named — **lost updates**, **read skew**, and **write skew** — and those are the ones that cause most production bugs. Moving up the spectrum adds guarantees but can reduce throughput. Understanding where your database sits on this spectrum, and when to change it, is fundamental backend engineering knowledge.

Modern databases like PostgreSQL implement these levels not with brute-force locking but with **Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)** — a sophisticated mechanism that keeps multiple row versions alive simultaneously, allowing readers and writers to proceed concurrently without blocking each other. Understanding MVCC unlocks intuition about why isolation behaves the way it does, why `autovacuum` matters, and what `transaction_id` wraparound means in production PostgreSQL.

flowchart TD
  A["Concurrent Transactions"] --> B["Anomaly Risk"]
  B --> C["Dirty Read"]
  B --> D["Non-Repeatable Read"]
  B --> E["Phantom Read"]
  C --> F["Read Uncommitted prevents nothing"]
  C --> G["Read Committed prevents dirty reads"]

sections.caption: The three classic concurrency anomalies and which isolation level prevents each. Every level prevents all anomalies of lower levels.

sections.title: The Whiteboard in the Conference Room
sections.content:
Picture a shared conference room whiteboard used by several colleagues throughout the day. Under **Read Uncommitted**, you can walk in and read your colleague's half-finished scribbles — equations crossed out, arrows half-drawn, partially erased notes. If they decide to wipe the board before finishing (a rollback), you have already based your work on data that never officially existed.

Under **Read Committed**, you can only read what has been finalized in permanent marker — anything still being sketched in pencil is invisible to you. Safe from erased guesses, but if the same colleague finalizes a different number between your two glances at the board, you may see contradictory values.

Under **Repeatable Read**, you take a photograph of the board the moment you enter the room. No matter how much colleagues erase and rewrite during your visit, you always consult your own snapshot. Consistent readings — but your photo can go stale. If you erase one item based on what your photo shows while a colleague erases a different item based on *their* photo, together you can leave the board in a state neither of you would have allowed (that is write skew).

Under **Serializable**, the end result must look as if only one person used the whiteboard at a time — door locked. A naive implementation really does lock the door, and throughput suffers. PostgreSQL is cleverer: it lets everyone in at once, watches who read what, and sends someone back out to redo their work only when the combined edits could not have happened one-at-a-time.

sections.title: The Three Anomalies: What Can Go Wrong
sections.content:
Before exploring the solutions it is important to understand the problems precisely. Each anomaly has a specific definition, not just a vague sense of 'something went wrong'.

**Dirty Read**: Transaction T2 reads a row that T1 has modified but not yet committed. If T1 subsequently rolls back, T2 has operated on data that never officially existed in the database. This is the most dangerous anomaly because the data T2 sees may be radically different from what ultimately gets committed — or may represent a state the database explicitly rejected.

Example: T1 transfers $500 from account A to account B: it debits A (balance drops to $0) but has not yet credited B. T2 reads A's balance mid-transaction and sees $0. T1 then rolls back due to a network error. The true balance of A is whatever it was before the transfer, but T2 has already made decisions based on $0.

**Non-Repeatable Read**: Within a single transaction, T1 reads the same row twice and gets different values because T2 committed a change between the two reads. The row is not dirty — T2 committed legitimately — but T1's two reads are inconsistent with each other. This matters whenever a transaction uses the same data in multiple steps, such as reading a value, computing something, then verifying the value is still what you expected.

Example: T1 reads a product's stock count (10 units) and decides to place an order. Before T1 commits, T2 sells the last 10 units and commits. T1 reads the stock count again to confirm (perhaps in a validation step) and sees 0. The same SELECT returned different values within one transaction.

**Phantom Read**: T1 runs a range query (e.g., `WHERE salary > 100000`) and gets 5 rows. T2 inserts a new employee with salary 150000 and commits. T1 runs the same range query again and now sees 6 rows. Unlike a non-repeatable read (same row, different value), a phantom involves new rows appearing in a range that was already scanned. The 'phantom' is the new row that materialized between two otherwise identical queries.

Phantom reads are subtler than they appear. Even if you prevent non-repeatable reads by locking individual rows, new rows can still be inserted between range scans because locks on existing rows do not prevent insertion of new ones. Preventing phantoms requires range-level locking or MVCC snapshot semantics that encompass the entire query predicate.

sections.title: Beyond the Standard: Lost Updates and Read Skew
sections.content:
The SQL-92 definitions were famously criticised in the 1995 paper *A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels* (Berenson, Bernstein, Gray and others) as ambiguous and incomplete. The paper named anomalies the standard ignores — and they are the ones that bite real applications:

**Lost update**: T1 and T2 both read `balance = 100`, each computes a new value in application code (100 + 10 and 100 + 20) and writes it back. The second write silently overwrites the first: the final balance is 120 instead of 130. Read Committed allows this. PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read prevents it — the second writer fails with `could not serialize access due to concurrent update` (SQLSTATE `40001`) — but **MySQL InnoDB's Repeatable Read does not**, because InnoDB `UPDATE`s act on the latest committed row rather than the transaction's snapshot.

**Read skew**: T1 reads account A (500). T2 then transfers 100 from A to B and commits. T1 reads account B (600) and concludes the total is 1,100 — a state that never existed (before: 1,000; after: 1,000). Read Committed allows it across statements; any snapshot-based level (Repeatable Read and above) prevents it. It matters for reports, backups (`pg_dump` uses a single snapshot for exactly this reason), and consistency checks.

**Write skew**: two transactions read overlapping data and then write *different* rows — covered in detail below, because snapshot isolation still allows it.

sections.label: Lost update fixes
sections.explanation: Fix 1 is the cheapest and should be your default: when two `balance = balance + 10` statements race at Read Committed, PostgreSQL makes the second one wait for the first, then re-evaluates it against the newly committed row, so both increments survive. Fix 2 is for logic too complex for one statement. Fix 3 avoids holding locks across user think-time (common in ORMs and HTTP APIs). Fix 4 works in PostgreSQL only — on MySQL InnoDB, Repeatable Read would let the lost update through, so use Fix 1–3 there.

sections.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant T1 as Transaction 1
  participant DB as Database
  participant T2 as Transaction 2
  T1->>DB: BEGIN
  T2->>DB: BEGIN
  T1->>DB: UPDATE balance=0 (uncommitted)
  T2->>DB: SELECT balance, sees 0 (dirty!)
  T1->>DB: ROLLBACK
  Note over T2: T2 acted on data that never committed
sections.caption: Dirty read: T2 sees T1's uncommitted write. When T1 rolls back, T2 has acted on a value that never existed. Every PostgreSQL isolation level prevents this.

sections.title: The Four Isolation Levels in Detail
sections.content:
**Read Uncommitted** is the weakest level. Transactions can see uncommitted changes from all other concurrent transactions. Dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads are all possible. This level is almost never used in production systems because the data seen may be inconsistent with what ever gets committed. (MySQL InnoDB and SQL Server do honour it, mostly for approximate monitoring queries.) PostgreSQL technically accepts this setting but actually implements it as Read Committed — it refuses to show uncommitted data even when asked.

**Read Committed** is the default in PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server. It prevents dirty reads by ensuring each statement sees only rows that were committed *before that statement began executing*. The critical nuance is that the snapshot is per-statement, not per-transaction. If you run two identical SELECT statements within one transaction, each takes a fresh snapshot — so committed changes from other transactions that occur between your two SELECTs will be visible in the second one. This is the source of non-repeatable reads and phantom reads at this level.

For the vast majority of OLTP workloads, Read Committed is sufficient. Most transactions are short-lived and do not rely on seeing the same data twice in the same transaction. The level provides a good balance of correctness and concurrency.

**Repeatable Read** takes one snapshot for the whole transaction — in PostgreSQL (and for MySQL's plain reads) at the transaction's *first statement*, not at `BEGIN` itself — and uses it for all reads throughout the transaction's lifetime. This prevents non-repeatable reads because the same row will always return the same value — it is always read from the same snapshot. According to the SQL standard, Repeatable Read still allows phantom reads (new rows inserted by others), but PostgreSQL's MVCC-based implementation also prevents phantom reads at this level as a side effect of snapshot isolation. This means PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read is actually stronger than the standard requires: it is **snapshot isolation**. It also prevents lost updates — if you try to update a row that another transaction changed after your snapshot, you get SQLSTATE `40001` and must retry, so retry logic is needed at this level too. What it still allows is **write skew**. MySQL InnoDB uses Repeatable Read as its *default* level, with different semantics (see the cross-database section below).

Use Repeatable Read when your transaction reads data multiple times and the consistency of those reads matters — financial report generation, complex multi-step validations, or any workflow where you read some data, compute something, then need to verify the underlying data has not changed.

**Serializable** is the gold standard. It guarantees that the outcome of any set of concurrent serializable transactions is identical to some serial (one-at-a-time) execution of those transactions. It prevents all three anomalies and additionally prevents subtler write-skew anomalies that MVCC snapshots alone cannot catch.

PostgreSQL implements Serializable using **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**, a relatively recent algorithm (first deployed in PostgreSQL 9.1, 2011) that tracks read and write dependencies between transactions. When it detects a cycle that would make the concurrent execution non-serializable, it aborts one transaction with `SQLSTATE 40001` (serialization_failure). Applications must be designed to retry on this error.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Read Uncommitted"] -->|"+ dirty read prevention"| B["Read Committed"]
  B -->|"+ non-repeatable read prevention"| C["Repeatable Read"]
  C -->|"+ phantom + write-skew prevention"| D["Serializable"]
  A --- E["Most concurrent / least safe"]
  D --- F["Least concurrent / most safe"]
sections.caption: The isolation spectrum. Each level is a strict superset of the guarantees below it. PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server default to Read Committed; MySQL InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read.

sections.title: MVCC: How PostgreSQL Implements Isolation Without Locking
sections.content:
Traditional databases enforced isolation with **locking**: readers acquire shared locks, writers acquire exclusive locks. A writer blocks readers; readers block writers. This serializes access to popular rows and tanks throughput under high concurrency.

PostgreSQL uses **Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)** instead. The core idea: rather than locking a row during modification, keep the old version alive and write a *new version* of the row. Readers read old versions; writers create new ones. Readers and writers never block each other.

Every row in PostgreSQL has two hidden system columns:
- **`xmin`**: the transaction ID (`xid`) of the transaction that created (inserted) this row version.
- **`xmax`**: the transaction ID of the transaction that deleted or superseded this row version. If `xmax` is 0 or refers to an aborted transaction, the row is still live.

A **snapshot** records which transactions had finished when it was taken: every xid below its `xmin` is finished, every xid at or above its `xmax` had not started, and a list (`xip`) holds those in progress in between. A row version is visible to me if (1) its `xmin` committed *before my snapshot* (not in progress, not aborted, not newer), and (2) its `xmax` is empty, belongs to an aborted transaction, or had not committed as of my snapshot. My own transaction's changes are always visible to me. Each isolation level defines what 'my snapshot' means — per-statement for Read Committed, per-transaction-start for Repeatable Read and Serializable.

When a transaction updates row R:
1. The old version gets its `xmax` set to the current transaction ID (marking it 'deleted by this transaction').
2. A new row version is inserted with `xmin` = current transaction ID.
3. Both versions coexist on the heap page until cleanup.

When the transaction commits, the new version becomes visible to subsequent snapshots. When it rolls back, the new version's `xmin` points to an aborted transaction, making it invisible — effectively erased without ever becoming visible.

**The cost of MVCC**: Old row versions (called **dead tuples**) accumulate on heap pages. They are not immediately removed because long-running transactions might still need to see them. The background **autovacuum** process periodically scans tables and reclaims space occupied by dead tuples that are no longer visible to any active transaction. If autovacuum cannot keep up (due to extremely long-running transactions or high write volume), tables bloat and query performance degrades. This is why `idle in transaction` connections are dangerous in production — they hold back the database-wide "xmin horizon", so autovacuum cannot reclaim *any* row version that died after that transaction began — in every table, not just the ones it touched.

sections.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant T1 as Reader (xid=100)
  participant Heap as Table Heap
  participant T2 as Writer (xid=101)
  T2->>Heap: UPDATE writes new version (xmin=101)
  T2->>Heap: Old version gets xmax=101
  T1->>Heap: SELECT
  Heap-->>T1: Old version (xmin=99 committed, xmax=101 still running)
  T2->>Heap: COMMIT
  T1->>Heap: Next SELECT (fresh snapshot at Read Committed)
  Heap-->>T1: New version (xmin=101 now committed)
sections.caption: MVCC in action: the writer creates a new row version while the reader continues to see the old one. No locks are held. At Read Committed, each new statement gets a fresh snapshot and may see the committed write.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
-- ── Setting isolation levels in PostgreSQL ──────────────────────────────

-- Set for a single transaction
BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;

  -- Both SELECTs use the SAME snapshot, taken at the first statement
  SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 42;   -- returns 1000

  -- Suppose another transaction commits: UPDATE accounts SET balance=750 WHERE id=42
  -- That commit happened AFTER our snapshot → invisible to us

  SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 42;   -- still 1000 (repeatable!)

COMMIT;


-- ── Demonstrating the phantom at Read Committed ──────────────────────────
BEGIN;  -- defaults to READ COMMITTED

  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';  -- returns 5

  -- Another transaction: INSERT INTO orders(status) VALUES ('pending'); COMMIT;

  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';  -- returns 6 (phantom!)
  -- Each statement took a NEW snapshot, so the inserted row is now visible

COMMIT;


-- ── Serializable: handles write-skew that snapshots miss ─────────────────
-- Scenario: two doctors both try to go off-call, but at least one must remain on-call
-- T1 reads: 2 on-call doctors. Decides it's safe to go off-call. Sets itself off-call.
-- T2 reads: 2 on-call doctors. Decides it's safe to go off-call. Sets itself off-call.
-- Outcome without Serializable: 0 on-call doctors — a write-skew anomaly.

BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call = true;  -- 2
  -- app: go off-call only if count >= 2 (someone else stays on call)
  UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false WHERE id = :my_id;  -- psql variable
COMMIT;
-- PostgreSQL detects the dangerous rw-dependency pattern and aborts one:
-- ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies
--         among transactions
-- SQLSTATE: 40001  → application MUST retry the whole transaction
sections.explanation: The first block shows Repeatable Read's per-transaction snapshot preventing non-repeatable reads. The second shows Read Committed's per-statement snapshot allowing phantoms. The third illustrates write-skew — a subtle anomaly only Serializable catches. Note that MVCC alone does not prevent write-skew; SSI's dependency tracking is required.

sections.title: Write-Skew: The Anomaly That Surprises Even Experts
sections.content:
Write-skew is perhaps the most counter-intuitive concurrency anomaly, and it is the primary reason Serializable exists beyond Repeatable Read.

**Definition**: Two transactions each read some shared data, then each writes a *different* row based on what it read — a write that would be invalid if it could see the other's write. Because their **write sets do not overlap**, snapshot isolation (which only detects write-write conflicts) lets both commit, yet the combined outcome violates an application invariant.

**Classic example — doctor on-call system**: A hospital requires that at least one doctor is always on call. Two doctors, Alice and Bob, both check the on-call list. Both see two people on call (themselves and each other). Both decide it is safe to mark themselves off-call. Each commits successfully. The result: zero doctors on call — a violated invariant.

Under Repeatable Read (MVCC snapshot isolation), this anomaly is possible because:
- Alice reads the on-call count: sees 2. Writes: marks herself off-call.
- Bob reads the on-call count: sees 2 (his snapshot was taken before Alice committed). Writes: marks himself off-call.
- Both commits succeed. Neither transaction wrote a row the other *wrote* (Alice updated her row, Bob updated his), so there is no write-write conflict. Each did write a row the other had *read* — that read/write dependency is exactly what Serializable tracks.

Serializable (SSI) prevents this by tracking **read/write anti-dependencies**. Alice must come before Bob (Bob's write changed something Alice read) *and* Bob must come before Alice (for the same reason in reverse) — no serial order can produce this result, so one transaction is aborted.

**Other write-skew scenarios**: booking systems where each booking is a new row (two users both see the room free for 3–5 pm, both insert overlapping bookings), uniqueness checks done in application code (both verify a username is free, both insert), and spending limits checked against a sum of rows (two withdrawals each see enough headroom).

**Fixes without Serializable**: lock the rows the decision depends on (`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`) — this only works when those rows already exist; for "check that nothing exists, then insert" there is nothing to lock, so use a **constraint** instead (`UNIQUE`, or an `EXCLUDE USING gist` constraint for overlapping time ranges) or **materialize the conflict** by creating a row to lock (for example one row per room per time slot).

sections.title: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: How PostgreSQL Detects Cycles
sections.content:
PostgreSQL's SSI implementation (by Kevin Grittner and Dan R. K. Ports, shipped in PostgreSQL 9.1 in 2011 and described in their 2012 VLDB paper) reasons about three types of dependencies between concurrent serializable transactions:

**rw-anti-dependency** (the critical one): Transaction T1 reads a version of a row, then T2 writes a new version of that same row. In a serial execution, either T1 ran first (before T2 wrote), or T1 ran after (and should have seen T2's write). An rw-anti-dependency means we are in the first scenario — T1 read data that T2 is about to supersede.

**ww-dependency**: T2 updates a row that T1 also updated. One of them 'wins'; both cannot be serialized in an order where neither overwrites the other.

**wr-dependency**: T1 reads data that T2 wrote. T2 must come first in any serial order.

A **cycle** in this dependency graph means no valid serial ordering exists. Tracking full cycles is expensive, so PostgreSQL uses the Cahill–Fekete shortcut: every non-serializable execution under snapshot isolation contains a **"dangerous structure"** — two consecutive rw-anti-dependencies T1 → T2 → T3 (T1 and T3 may be the same transaction). When PostgreSQL sees one, it aborts a not-yet-committed participant, chosen so that an immediate retry will not hit the same conflict. The check is conservative: it can abort transactions that would actually have been serializable (**false positives**), but it never lets a real anomaly through.

**Application responsibility**: Because serialization failures are expected and not bugs, applications using Serializable isolation must implement retry logic. The typical pattern is a loop: begin, execute business logic, attempt commit, catch `SQLSTATE 40001`, and repeat. Exponential backoff helps if contention is high. Most ORMs and connection pool libraries support retry hooks for exactly this purpose.

**Performance implications**: SSI has overhead because the database tracks additional metadata (SIREAD locks — special locks on the data ranges read, not real locks that block writers). This metadata grows with the number of concurrent serializable transactions and with the volume of data they read. SIREAD locks are kept per row, but are promoted to page or whole-table granularity when there are many of them (and a sequential scan locks the whole table), which raises the false-positive abort rate. For short transactions that read through indexes, the overhead versus Repeatable Read is usually modest; for long transactions scanning large data sets, both the tracking cost and the abort rate can be significant. Declaring read-only work `READ ONLY` (and `DEFERRABLE` for long reports) lets PostgreSQL skip much of it.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  T1["T1 Alice: reads on-call rows, sets Alice off"]
  T2["T2 Bob: reads on-call rows, sets Bob off"]
  T1 -->|"rw: T1 read Bob's row, T2 wrote it"| T2
  T2 -->|"rw: T2 read Alice's row, T1 wrote it"| T1
  T1 --> D["Cycle: no serial order explains both results"]
  T2 --> D
  D --> E["SSI aborts one with SQLSTATE 40001"]
sections.caption: Write skew as a dependency graph: each transaction read a row the other wrote, so each must come before the other. SSI detects the pattern and aborts one; the retry then sees the other doctor already off call.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
-- ── Inspecting MVCC internals in PostgreSQL ─────────────────────────────

-- See the hidden xmin/xmax on every row
SELECT xmin, xmax, id, balance
FROM accounts
WHERE id = 42;
-- xmin: transaction that created this version
-- xmax: transaction that deleted/updated this version (0 if still live)

-- Current transaction ID (PostgreSQL 13+; older: txid_current())
SELECT pg_current_xact_id();

-- See what your current snapshot looks like
SELECT pg_current_snapshot();   -- older: txid_current_snapshot()
-- Returns something like: 1234:1240:1234,1237
-- Format: xmin:xmax:xip_list
-- xmin = lowest xid still in progress (everything below is finished)
-- xmax = first xid not yet assigned (everything >= is invisible)
-- xip_list = xids in progress when the snapshot was taken

-- Check current isolation level
SHOW transaction_isolation;

-- Set default for the session
SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;

-- See dead tuples accumulating (before autovacuum runs)
SELECT schemaname, relname, n_dead_tup, n_live_tup, last_autovacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE relname = 'accounts';

-- Find sessions holding back cleanup
SELECT pid, state, xact_start, backend_xmin
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
ORDER BY xact_start;

-- ── Retry pattern for Serializable (application layer) ───────────────────
-- (Pseudocode in SQL comment form — real retry belongs in app code)
-- LOOP:
--   BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
--   ... business logic ...
--   COMMIT;
--   EXIT loop on success;
--   ON SQLSTATE '40001': -- serialization_failure
--     ROLLBACK;
--     CONTINUE loop; -- retry
-- END LOOP
sections.explanation: The xmin/xmax columns expose MVCC internals that are normally hidden. `pg_current_snapshot()` shows your snapshot's boundaries — useful for debugging visibility questions. Note that `pg_stat_user_tables` names the table column `relname`, not `tablename`. High `n_dead_tup` with a stale `last_autovacuum` means autovacuum is falling behind; the `pg_stat_activity` query finds the long-open transactions that are usually the cause.

sections.title: Practical Guidance: Choosing the Right Level
sections.content:
The right isolation level depends on what your transaction is doing and what invariants it must maintain. Here is a practical decision framework:

**Use Read Committed (the default) when**: your transactions are short, each statement stands alone, and you do not rely on seeing the same data twice in one transaction. This covers the vast majority of web application operations — inserting a record, updating a row, reading a list of items for display. PostgreSQL's default is Read Committed for good reason. Read-modify-write still needs care at this level: use atomic updates (`SET stock = stock - 1`), `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, or optimistic version checks to avoid lost updates.

**Upgrade to Repeatable Read when**: a transaction reads data in one place and uses that data to make decisions that depend on the data not changing by the time the transaction commits. Classic examples: financial reporting transactions that read multiple tables and produce aggregate results, inventory allocation (read available stock, compute allocation, write), or any multi-step workflow that must act on a consistent view of data. In PostgreSQL, be ready to retry on SQLSTATE `40001` here too — a concurrent update to a row you also update aborts your transaction.

**Use Serializable when**: your application enforces invariants that span multiple rows and multiple transactions, and those invariants cannot be expressed as simple unique constraints or foreign keys. The doctor on-call example, double-booking prevention for a finite resource, and balance-at-most-X constraints are all good candidates. Accept the retry burden — it is manageable and the correctness guarantee is valuable.

**Never use Read Uncommitted** in production. The potential for dirty reads introduces correctness bugs that are extremely difficult to diagnose because they are timing-dependent and intermittent.

**Transaction length matters as much as isolation level**: A long-running transaction at Read Committed holds a snapshot that blocks autovacuum from reclaiming dead tuples from the beginning of that snapshot. Connections left `idle in transaction` are a common production antipattern — they hold snapshots indefinitely, causing table bloat and eventually degrading query performance database-wide. Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` in PostgreSQL to automatically terminate stale transactions.

sections.title: Isolation Levels Across Different Databases
sections.content:
Different database systems implement the SQL standard differently, and the same level name can mean different things across systems.

**PostgreSQL**: Read Committed (default, MVCC per-statement snapshot), Repeatable Read (MVCC per-transaction snapshot — stronger than standard, also prevents phantoms), Serializable (SSI). Does not implement Read Uncommitted differently from Read Committed.

**MySQL InnoDB**: Read Committed (per-statement snapshot), **Repeatable Read (the default)**, Serializable (uses locking rather than SSI — plain SELECTs become shared-lock reads, blocking writers). InnoDB's Repeatable Read is a hybrid: plain `SELECT`s read a per-transaction snapshot (no phantoms there), but `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, and locking reads (`FOR UPDATE` / `FOR SHARE`) operate on the **latest committed** rows and take next-key (row + gap) locks. So a transaction can see a row in its snapshot that its own `UPDATE` then finds changed — and lost updates are not detected the way PostgreSQL detects them.

**Oracle**: Only supports Read Committed (default) and Serializable. There is no Repeatable Read in Oracle — Serializable is the next step up. Oracle's Serializable is actually snapshot isolation, not true serializability by the strict definition, though it prevents most common anomalies.

**SQL Server**: Supports all four standard levels plus two additional non-standard snapshot modes. `READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT` (RCSI) makes Read Committed use row versioning instead of shared locks — important because classic SQL Server Read Committed uses shared locks that make readers and writers block each other. RCSI is off by default for on-premises SQL Server but on by default in Azure SQL Database. The separate `SNAPSHOT` level gives transaction-level snapshot isolation.

**Practical implication**: When reading documentation or Stack Overflow answers about isolation levels, always check which database is being discussed. 'Repeatable Read prevents phantoms' is true in PostgreSQL, only partly true in MySQL (plain snapshot reads yes, locking reads see new rows), and not required by the SQL standard.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Which isolation level?"] --> B["Transaction reads same data twice?"]  
  B -->|"No"| C["Read Committed (default)"]
  B -->|"Yes"| D["Invariant spans multiple rows or transactions?"]
  D -->|"No"| E["Repeatable Read"]
  D -->|"Yes"| F["Serializable + retry logic"]
  F --> G["Implement SQLSTATE 40001 retry"]
sections.caption: Decision tree for choosing an isolation level. Most applications stay at Read Committed; escalate only when your transaction's correctness requires it.

sections.content: **Historical context**: MVCC was first proposed by David P. Reed in his 1978 MIT PhD thesis. Oracle was among the first commercial databases to implement it (mid-1980s). PostgreSQL adopted MVCC in version 6.5 (1999). The SSI algorithm that powers PostgreSQL's Serializable level was published by Michael J. Cahill, Uwe Rohm, and Alan D. Fekete in their 2008 SIGMOD paper 'Serializable Isolation for Snapshot Databases' — it showed for the first time that true serializability could be implemented on top of snapshot isolation at acceptable overhead. MySQL InnoDB's approach uses traditional locking for gap-range phantom prevention, making it fundamentally different under the hood despite using similar level names.

**Common mistakes and interview insights**: (1) Confusing the *count* of anomalies a level prevents with the *strength* of its guarantee — Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL is stronger than the SQL standard says it must be. (2) Assuming Serializable is 'too slow to use' — for short, index-driven transactions SSI overhead is usually modest, and the correctness benefit is substantial for invariant-critical code; measure your own abort rate. (3) Forgetting that long-running transactions at *any* level cause table bloat via MVCC dead tuples — isolation level and transaction duration are separate knobs. (4) Not handling `SQLSTATE 40001` at Serializable — this is not an error to bubble to the user; it is a normal occurrence requiring a retry. (5) Assuming MySQL's default Repeatable Read behaves like PostgreSQL's — it does not detect lost updates, so use atomic updates or `FOR UPDATE`. (6) On interviews: when asked 'how does MVCC work?' the key answer is: 'each row has xmin/xmax transaction IDs; readers filter by their snapshot without acquiring locks; writers create new versions; dead versions are cleaned by autovacuum.'

items: **Three classic anomalies**: dirty reads (seeing uncommitted data), non-repeatable reads (same row, different values in one transaction), and phantom reads (range queries returning new rows). Each higher isolation level prevents an additional anomaly.
**Read Committed** (default in PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server) takes a fresh snapshot per statement — prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads, phantoms, read skew, and lost updates.

**Repeatable Read** (MySQL InnoDB's default) uses one snapshot per transaction. In PostgreSQL it is snapshot isolation: no phantoms, lost updates abort with 40001 — but write skew is still possible. InnoDB's version lets UPDATEs see the latest rows, so lost updates slip through.
**Lost update** is the most common real-world race: read a value, compute in the app, write it back. Fix with atomic `SET x = x + 1`, `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, or an optimistic version column.

**Serializable** prevents all anomalies including write-skew (two transactions each read and write in ways that are individually valid but collectively violate invariants). PostgreSQL uses SSI, aborting transactions with `SQLSTATE 40001`; applications must implement retry logic.

**Write skew without Serializable**: lock the rows the decision depends on (`FOR UPDATE`), or — when the conflict is about rows that do not exist yet — use a `UNIQUE`/`EXCLUDE` constraint or materialize a row to lock.

**MVCC** avoids read/write locking by tagging each row version with `xmin` (creator transaction ID) and `xmax` (deleting transaction ID). Readers filter by their snapshot's transaction ID; writers create new versions. This is why readers and writers do not block each other in PostgreSQL.

**Dead tuples** accumulate under MVCC and are reclaimed by autovacuum. Long-running or `idle in transaction` connections prevent autovacuum from cleaning old versions, causing table bloat and performance degradation — set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` to mitigate.

**Isolation level names are not portable**: PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read prevents phantoms, MySQL's does not by the same mechanism, and Oracle calls its next-level Serializable (which is actually snapshot isolation). Always check database-specific behavior.

quiz.question: Which isolation level allows a transaction to read uncommitted changes from another transaction, potentially reading data that will later be rolled back?
quiz.explanation: Read Uncommitted is the weakest level and permits dirty reads — a transaction can see changes that another transaction has not yet committed and may still roll back, meaning the data seen may never officially exist.

quiz.question: Transaction T1 reads the same row twice within a single transaction and gets different values because T2 committed a change between the two reads. This anomaly is called:
quiz.explanation: A non-repeatable read happens when the same SELECT within one transaction returns different values for an existing row because another committed transaction modified that row between the two reads.

quiz.question: Under Read Committed isolation, why can two identical SELECT COUNT(*) queries in the same transaction return different values?
options: Each statement takes a fresh snapshot, so rows committed between the two queries become visible
Read Committed allows dirty reads from other transactions
The query planner caches and then invalidates the first result
quiz.explanation: Read Committed takes a new snapshot per statement, not per transaction. If another transaction inserts rows and commits between your two COUNT queries, the second query's snapshot includes those rows — a phantom read.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between how MVCC handles reads vs. the traditional locking approach?
options: MVCC queues reads behind writes to ensure sequential access
MVCC copies the entire table to a read buffer at transaction start
MVCC keeps multiple row versions so readers get a snapshot without blocking writers
MVCC uses shared locks that readers acquire without blocking other readers
quiz.explanation: MVCC stores multiple versions of each row tagged with transaction IDs. Readers find the appropriate version for their snapshot without acquiring locks, so they never block writers and writers never block readers.

quiz.question: Two doctors both check the on-call list (seeing 2 on-call), both decide it's safe to go off-call, and both commit — leaving 0 doctors on call. Which anomaly is this?
quiz.explanation: Write-skew occurs when two transactions each read shared data, then each writes to different rows in a way that is valid in isolation but collectively violates an application invariant. Their write sets do not overlap, so snapshot isolation (which only checks write-write conflicts) misses it; only Serializable, which tracks read/write dependencies, catches it.

quiz.question: A transaction at Serializable isolation level fails with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure). What is the correct application response?
options: Escalate to a higher isolation level
Retry the entire transaction from the beginning
Report the error to the user and abort permanently
Switch to Read Committed and retry the failed statement only
quiz.explanation: Serialization failures are expected and normal with Serializable isolation — they indicate that concurrent execution would produce a non-serializable result. The correct response is to retry the entire transaction; the retry will typically succeed once the conflicting transaction has completed.

quiz.question: In PostgreSQL's MVCC implementation, what do the hidden `xmin` and `xmax` columns on a row tuple represent?
options: The transaction IDs of the transactions that created and deleted/updated this row version
The minimum and maximum values stored in the row
The first and last timestamps when the row was accessed
The transaction IDs of the oldest and newest concurrent readers
quiz.explanation: xmin is the transaction ID of the transaction that inserted this row version; xmax is the transaction ID of the transaction that deleted or superseded it (0 if still live). These are used to determine row visibility for each transaction's snapshot.

quiz.question: What PostgreSQL background process is responsible for reclaiming storage occupied by dead MVCC row versions?
quiz.explanation: Autovacuum reclaims storage occupied by dead tuples — old row versions whose xmax transaction has committed and which are no longer visible to any active transaction snapshot. Without autovacuum, tables grow unboundedly under heavy write workloads.

quiz.question: According to the SQL standard, which isolation level is the minimum required to prevent phantom reads?
quiz.explanation: The SQL standard requires only Serializable to prevent phantom reads. Repeatable Read is only required to prevent dirty reads and non-repeatable reads. However, PostgreSQL's MVCC-based Repeatable Read also prevents phantoms in practice — stronger than the standard mandates.

quiz.question: Why are long-running transactions or connections left 'idle in transaction' dangerous in a PostgreSQL production system?
options: They hold a snapshot that prevents autovacuum from cleaning dead tuples, causing table bloat
They consume extra CPU cycles running periodic snapshot refreshes
They hold exclusive locks that block all other reads and writes
They force all new transactions to use Serializable isolation
quiz.explanation: A long-running transaction holds an open MVCC snapshot. Autovacuum cannot reclaim dead tuples that are still visible to any active snapshot, so tables accumulate dead row versions (bloat) for as long as that transaction stays open — eventually degrading query performance across the entire database.
